newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Peters' New Zealand pension plan takes a body blow.
newsitem.headline: Peters' New Zealand pension plan takes a body blow.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer Winston Peters' push for compulsory pensions suffered a big blow on Thursday when a review group favoured the current scheme.
A task force charged with reviewing the current taxpayer-funded scheme, known as New Zealand Super (NZS) said it could be maintained with gradual changes.
Peters, leader of the junior party in the conservative government coalition, New Zealand First, has hung his hat on a compulsory scheme, saying the present scheme is unsustainable.
It is seen as a defining issue for the populist Peters and his party, who have seen their support plummet since signing the coalition deal in December.
A referendum on Peters' scheme will be held in September.
Prime Minister Jim Bolger has drawn criticism from his own backbenchers, who overwhelmingly oppose compulsion, and raised questions about his future leadership.

In parliament on Thursday, National backbencher John Banks asked Bolger: "Does the Prime Minister yet understand and accept that people who know something about these matters don't agree with him, and when will he give away his uninformed support for this fatally flawed proposal or is it a case of where Winston goes, I go?"
Leadership aspirant Jenny Shipley, the state services minister, has also made strong play of her opposition to the scheme.
Opposition politicians said Thursday's report effectively undermined Peters' plan.

"It is not the final nail in the coffin of the plan -- that has already been driven in. It is the largest lump of earth descending on the coffin as it goes down," Labour's finance spokesman Michael Cullen said.
But Peters was unfazed, welcoming the report as confirming the current pay-as-you-go pension scheme was unsustainable.
"It's crunch time now. Tell New Zealanders with precision what they will get and how they will get it," Peters challenged his critics.
But he refused to be drawn on what he would advocate if the referendum rejected his compulsory scheme.
Opinion polls indicate the compulsory scheme, which would require savings funded by broadly equivalent tax cuts to be invested in an annuity, will be overwhelmingly rejected.
The task force report concluded that the current superannuation scheme was sustainable with some gradual changes to meet the demands placed on it by an ageing population after 2015.

"The tide is coming in but it is not an unexpected or unpredictable tsunami," said Jeff Todd, the Auckland accountant chairing the task force. "Careful preparation is needed, but we don't need to dismantle what we have in place."
As baby boomers retire in increasing numbers the costs will rise to nine percent of GDP by 2050 from four percent at present.
"We don't think this will create an economic crisis though. Many other OECD countries are facing even stronger pressures on their public pension schemes," Todd said.

Options for ensuring NZS remained affordable included reducing debt levels now, raising the age of eligibility, and paying less publicly provided superannuation to those who could provide for themselves in retirement.
